overview.title: Overlaying the peach mask and prompting a banana
overview.subsection: 11.3.4 Prompting the model with a target point
overview.main_topic: Displaying SAM's first candidate mask on the image (Figure 11.11), then repeating the whole point-prompt pipeline with a new point (300, 550) on a banana.
overview.central_idea: Once `get_mask` and the display utilities exist, segmenting any object is a three-step routine: choose a labeled point, call `model.predict`, extract and overlay a mask. Only the point coordinates change between objects.
overview.importance: It demonstrates that SAM segments arbitrary objects with no task-specific training, and it sets up the banana example whose ambiguity motivates looking at the alternative masks on p.350.
learning_objectives: Compose show_image, show_mask and show_points on one Matplotlib axis to visualize a segmentation.
Read Figure 11.11 and relate the star position to the coordinates (580, 450).
Reproduce the full point-prompt pipeline for a new object.
Explain why the second banana, not the first, is selected by the point (300, 550).
prerequisites: get_mask and the SAM predict call (p.348)

summary:
The page completes the peach example begun on p.348. A short code block creates a 10 × 10-inch figure, draws the image, overlays the boolean `mask` returned by `get_mask(outputs, index=0)`, and marks the prompt point. **Figure 11.11, "Segmented peach"**, shows the result: a semi-transparent blue region covering exactly the red fruit under the green star at (580, 450), with the neighbouring apple, the yellow fruit the book later calls a mango (p.351) and the bowl left uncovered. The authors' verdict: "Pretty good!"

The text then moves to a second object, a banana. The new prompt point is `(300, 550)`, which lands on the **second banana from the left**. The listing repeats every step from scratch:

- `input_point = np.array([[300, 550]])` and `input_label = np.array([1])` (one foreground point),
- the same `model.predict` call with the `images`, `points` and `labels` dict, each with a batch axis,
- `mask = get_mask(outputs, index=0)` to extract the first candidate,
- the same four plotting lines as the peach example.

The output of this listing, Figure 11.12 ("Segmented banana"), appears at the top of the next page (p.350). The repetition makes the key point implicitly: nothing about the model or the post-processing is object-specific. Changing two numbers, the x and y of the prompt, retargets the segmentation. Coordinates are in the padded 1024 × 1024 frame, with x measured to the right and y measured downward, which is why (300, 550) falls in the lower-left area of the image where the bananas lie.

paragraphs.what_it_says: The authors' assessment of Figure 11.11: the peach mask is a good segmentation.
paragraphs.what_it_means: From one click and no training, SAM produced a mask that follows the outline of the peach and stops at the boundary with the adjacent apple and the bowl, which is a hard case because the fruits touch and have similar colours.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Compare with the model trained from scratch in 11.2 (p.338-341), which needed a labeled dataset and training; SAM's quality comes from large-scale pretraining on SA-1B (p.343).
connections: p.343: SAM's capability largely comes from the scale of the SA-1B pretraining dataset.

paragraphs.excerpt: Next, let’s try a banana. We’ll prompt the model with coordinates
paragraphs.what_it_says: A second test: the point (300, 550) lands on the second banana from the left; the result will be Figure 11.12.
paragraphs.what_it_means: In the padded image, x = 300 is about 30% of the way across and y = 550 slightly below the middle, which is on the right-hand of the two bananas. The two bananas touch at their stems, making this a slightly ambiguous prompt: one banana, or the pair?
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This example is chosen to show ambiguity. Candidate 0 picks a single banana (p.350, Figure 11.12), while other candidates include both (p.350-351).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Coordinates follow the image/Matplotlib convention: (x, y) = (column, row) with the origin at the top-left; the y axis in the figures grows downward.

concepts.name: Point prompt
concepts.definition: Labeled (x, y) coordinates telling SAM which object to segment.
concepts.technical: points (batch, n_points, 2), labels (batch, n_points) with 1 = foreground, 0 = background.
concepts.significance: Retargeting segmentation requires only changing the point.
concepts.misconception: The point need not be at the object's center; any pixel inside it works, because training sampled random pixels inside masks (p.345).

concepts.name: Mask overlay visualization
concepts.definition: Drawing a semi-transparent coloured mask on top of an image to inspect a segmentation.
concepts.intuition: Like a highlighter pen over the selected object.
concepts.technical: show_mask (p.347) multiplies the (h, w, 1) boolean mask by an RGBA colour (30, 144, 255)/255 with alpha 0.6, producing an (h, w, 4) image that Matplotlib composites over the photo on the same axis.
concepts.significance: Visual inspection is the quickest way to judge mask quality when no ground truth exists.
concepts.misconception: Pixels outside the mask are transparent (alpha 0), so they do not darken the image.

concepts.name: Segment Anything Model (SAM)
concepts.definition: Pretrained promptable segmentation model (Meta AI) used in section 11.3.
concepts.technical: Same predict call for any object; only the prompt changes.
concepts.significance: Zero training needed for new objects.
concepts.example: Peach and banana segmented with identical code.
concepts.misconception: SAM does not know the object is a 'banana'; it only outputs pixels.

code.title: Prompting SAM with a point on the banana
code.original_code:
input_point = np.array([[300, 550]])
input_label = np.array([1])

outputs = model.predict(
    {
        "images": ops.expand_dims(image, axis=0),
        "points": ops.expand_dims(input_point, axis=0),
        "labels": ops.expand_dims(input_label, axis=0),
    }
)
mask = get_mask(outputs, index=0)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 10))
show_image(image, plt.gca())
show_mask(mask, plt.gca())
show_points(input_point, plt.gca())
plt.show()

deeper.title: Why touching objects are hard and why SAM manages
deeper.body: The peach touches the apple and both are red, so colour alone cannot separate them; a simple threshold or flood-fill would leak across. SAM's image encoder has learned shape and boundary cues from ~100 masks per image across 11 million images (p.342-343), so it finds the contour between the two fruits. Beyond the book: segmenting touching instances of similar appearance is exactly what instance segmentation (p.334) is about.

deeper.title: Reading coordinates off the figures
deeper.body: The axes in Figures 11.10-11.12 run 0-1000+ for both x (left to right) and y (top to bottom). The black bands at the top (y < ~125) and bottom (y > ~900) are padding from resize_and_pad. The peach star at (580, 450) and the banana star at (300, 550) can be located directly on these axes.

misconceptions.correction: Only the prompt changes; the model and code are identical for the peach and the banana.

misconceptions.claim: Mask index 0 always captures the 'whole' object the user had in mind.
misconceptions.correction: For ambiguous prompts other candidates may be more appropriate, as shown with the two bananas on p.350.

questions.question: What changes between the peach example and the banana example?
questions.explanation: The banana listing reuses the same image, model, predict call, get_mask and plotting code; only input_point changes from (580, 450) to (300, 550). The label stays 1.

questions.question: What does `plt.gca()` return and why is it passed to every helper?
questions.answer: The current Matplotlib axis; passing the same axis lets image, mask and points be drawn on top of each other in one plot.
questions.explanation: The helpers on p.347 all take an `ax` argument so they can write to the same figure.

questions.question: Why is the banana a more interesting test of SAM than the peach?
questions.answer: The two bananas touch and look alike, so a point on one could mean 'this banana' or 'the bananas'; this ambiguity is what the multiple candidate masks address.
questions.explanation: On p.350-351 the alternative masks show the model offering both interpretations.

questions.question: If you accidentally wrote input_point = np.array([[550, 300]]), where would the point land?
options: On the same banana, since order does not matter
Higher up and further right, around the bowl and fruit
questions.answer: Higher up and further right, around the bowl and fruit
questions.explanation: x = 550 is right of center and y = 300 is in the upper half, which in Figure 11.11 is the bowl region near the yellow fruit (the "mango" of p.351). It is inside the image, and well above the bottom padding.

questions.question: Why does the banana listing call get_mask with index=0, and what would index=3 give?
questions.answer: index=0 takes the first candidate; index=3 would take the last of the four alternative masks, which may represent a different granularity of the object.
questions.explanation: outputs["masks"] holds four candidates (p.348). The next page plots indices 1-3.

questions.question: Can you predict what a point placed on the yellow fruit at the top of the bowl (the mango of p.351) would produce, and write the code for it?
questions.answer: Change input_point to a coordinate on that fruit (for example around (650, 300), inside the p.351 box) and rerun the same listing; the first mask should cover it.
questions.explanation: Tests whether you understood that only the prompt changes. The coordinate is an estimate from the figure.
